The net reactance is 62.8 minus 159.2, which is minus 96.4 ohms, so the circuit is net capacitive at this frequency, dominated by the capacitor because the frequency is below resonance. The impedance is 50 - j96.4, with magnitude the square root of 2500 plus 9293, about 108.6 ohms, at an angle of arctangent(-96.4/50), about minus 62.6 degrees. The current is 10 divided by 108.6, about 92.1 milliamps, leading the source voltage by 62.6 degrees. The individual component voltages follow from multiplying that current by each impedance: 4.6 volts across the resistor, in phase with the current; 5.79 volts across the inductor, leading the current by 90 degrees; and 14.66 volts across the capacitor, lagging by 90 degrees. Those three numbers, 4.6, 5.79 and 14.66, sum arithmetically to 25.05 volts, which is two and a half times the 10-volt source. Nothing is wrong. They must be added as phasors, and because the inductor and capacitor voltages are exactly 180 degrees apart they partly cancel, leaving a net reactive voltage of 14.66 minus 5.79, or 8.87 volts, at right angles to the resistor's 4.6 volts. The square root of 4.6 squared plus 8.87 squared is 9.99 volts, the source voltage, as Kirchhoff's law demands. This is the single most important lesson of alternating-current work and the one that most often catches out a beginner with a multimeter. Component voltages in a reactive circuit do not add arithmetically, and individual reactive voltages can substantially exceed the supply. Near resonance the excess becomes extreme, and a capacitor rated comfortably for the supply voltage can be destroyed by the voltage that appears across it. Sweeping the frequency reveals the full character of the circuit. Well below 1592 hertz the capacitive term grows without bound and the current tends to zero: the capacitor is blocking. Well above it the inductive term dominates and the current again falls: the inductor is choking. At exactly the frequency where the two match, the reactance vanishes altogether. The impedance curve is therefore a V, with a floor equal to R, and the phase swings from nearly plus 90 degrees of current lead at low frequency, through zero at the bottom of the V, to nearly 90 degrees of lag at high frequency. Every property of a tuned circuit is contained in that single picture.

sections.heading: Real Power, Reactive Power and Power Factor
sections.body: Because voltage and current are generally out of step, calculating power in an alternating circuit requires more care than multiplying two meter readings. Instantaneous power is always the product of instantaneous voltage and current, but when they are out of phase that product is negative during part of each cycle, meaning energy is flowing back from the circuit to the source. Averaging over a cycle gives the real power P = V*I*cos(phi), measured in watts, where V and I are RMS values and phi is the phase angle between them. The factor cos(phi) is the power factor. Only real power does useful work or produces heat, and only real power is billed to a domestic customer. The product V*I without the cosine is the apparent power S, measured in volt-amperes rather than watts to keep the distinction visible. It represents what the wires, transformers and switchgear must actually carry. The remaining component, Q = V*I*sin(phi), is the reactive power, measured in volt-amperes reactive, or VAR. It represents energy shuttling back and forth between the source and the circuit's magnetic and electric fields, doing no net work but consuming conductor capacity and causing real resistive losses along the way. The three relate as a right triangle, S squared equals P squared plus Q squared, and the whole picture is often drawn as the power triangle. A concrete illustration shows why utilities care. An industrial motor drawing 100 amps at 400 volts with a power factor of 0.7 lagging, typical of a lightly loaded induction motor, has an apparent power of 40 kilovolt-amperes but a real power of only 28 kilowatts. The cabling and transformer must be sized for 100 amps while the customer's useful work corresponds to only 70. The resistive losses in the supply network go as current squared, so the wasted heat is roughly double what it would be at unity power factor. Large consumers are therefore billed on apparent power or penalised for poor power factor. Correction is straightforward in principle. Since inductive loads make current lag and capacitors make it lead, connecting the right capacitance in parallel with an inductive load supplies the reactive power locally, so it circulates between load and capacitor rather than travelling back down the supply line. Correcting the motor above from 0.7 to 0.95 requires about 19.4 kilovolt-amperes reactive of capacitance, and reduces the line current from 100 amps to about 74. The subtlety worth flagging is that on modern loads with non-sinusoidal currents, such as switch-mode supplies and variable-speed drives, the displacement power factor described here is only part of the story; harmonic distortion also degrades the true power factor, and naively adding capacitors to such a system can excite a resonance and make matters considerably worse.

sections.heading: Frequency Response, Decibels and Bode Plots
sections.body: Because impedance depends on frequency, so does the behaviour of any circuit containing reactance. The natural way to describe that behaviour is the transfer function, written H(j*omega), defined as the output phasor divided by the input phasor. Being complex, it has a magnitude, telling how much the circuit scales the signal, and an angle, telling how much it shifts the timing. Plotting both against frequency characterises the circuit completely, at least for linear operation. The standard presentation, introduced by Hendrik Bode at Bell Labs in the 1930s and 1940s, uses logarithmic axes for both frequency and magnitude. Frequency runs logarithmically because circuits of interest span many orders of magnitude and because equal ratios of frequency, an octave being a factor of two and a decade a factor of ten, produce equal effects. Magnitude is expressed in decibels, computed as 20 times the base-ten logarithm of the voltage ratio. The factor of 20 rather than 10 appears because the decibel is fundamentally a power ratio and power goes as voltage squared. Useful landmarks: a voltage ratio of 2 is about 6 dB, a ratio of 10 is exactly 20 dB, a ratio of 0.707 is minus 3 dB, and a ratio of 0.5 is minus 6 dB. Consider the simplest possible case, a resistor in series with a capacitor with the output taken across the capacitor. Applying the voltage divider with complex impedances gives H = (1/(j*omega*C)) divided by (R + 1/(j*omega*C)), which simplifies to 1/(1 + j*omega*R*C). At very low frequency the term j*omega*R*C is negligible, H is approximately 1, and the output equals the input. At very high frequency that term dominates and the magnitude falls as 1 over omega*R*C, which on logarithmic axes is a straight line descending at 20 dB per decade, equivalently 6 dB per octave. The two straight-line asymptotes meet where omega*R*C equals 1, defining the corner or cutoff frequency, fc = 1/(2*pi*R*C). At that frequency the actual magnitude is 1 over the square root of 2, exactly minus 3 dB, and the output power is half the input power, which is why it is also called the half-power point. Phase tells a parallel story that is often more revealing. At low frequency the phase shift is zero, at the corner it is exactly minus 45 degrees, and far above it approaches minus 90 degrees, with the transition spread over about two decades. For a 10-kilohm resistor and a 15.9-nanofarad capacitor the corner sits at 1 kilohertz. This asymptotic sketching method is what makes Bode plots so useful in practice: a competent engineer can draw a usable frequency response for a moderately complex network in a minute, without computing a single point, simply by locating the corner frequencies and adding slopes.

sections.heading: Filters: Shaping the Spectrum
sections.body: A filter is any circuit whose transfer function deliberately favours some frequencies over others, and the simplest useful ones are two-component dividers. Swapping which element the output is taken across inverts the behaviour. Resistor in series with capacitor, output across the capacitor, gives a low-pass response: low frequencies pass, high frequencies are attenuated, because the capacitor's impedance falls with frequency and progressively shorts the output. Take the output across the resistor instead and the same two components form a high-pass filter. The corner frequency, 1/(2*pi*R*C), is identical either way. The same pair of possibilities exists for a resistor and inductor, with the roles reversed and the corner at R/(2*pi*L). These first-order filters have gentle skirts, rolling off at 20 dB per decade, which is often inadequate. Cascading sections steepens the slope by 20 dB per decade for each additional reactive element, but naively cascading two RC sections does not simply double the response, because the second section loads the first. Either the sections must be separated by a buffer amplifier or the loading must be accounted for, which is one reason active filters using operational amplifiers became standard. Combining an inductor and a capacitor gives a second-order response with a 40 dB per decade slope from just two reactive components, and additionally allows a peak near the corner. Beyond simple low-pass and high-pass lie two further shapes. A band-pass filter passes a band and rejects everything outside it, and can be built as a series LC in the signal path, whose impedance is minimum at resonance, or as a cascade of a high-pass and a low-pass with the high-pass corner below the low-pass corner. A band-stop or notch filter does the reverse, and is the tool of choice for removing a single interfering frequency such as 50-hertz mains hum from an instrumentation signal. Real filter design involves trade-offs that have been formalised into named families, each optimising something different at the expense of something else. The Butterworth response, described by Stephen Butterworth in 1930, is maximally flat in the passband with a moderate transition. The Chebyshev response achieves a steeper transition by tolerating ripple in the passband, with more ripple buying more steepness. The elliptic or Cauer response is steeper still, with ripple in both passband and stopband. The Bessel response sacrifices steepness for a maximally linear phase, meaning all frequencies are delayed equally, which preserves the shape of pulses and matters greatly in data and video work. No family is best; they trade amplitude flatness, transition steepness and phase linearity against each other, and choosing among them is the substance of filter design. One practical warning applies to all of them. A filter's published response assumes specified source and load impedances, and connecting one between arbitrary impedances shifts the corner frequency and can destroy the shape entirely. A passive LC filter designed for 50 ohms at both ends will misbehave badly if driven from a high-impedance source or loaded by an open circuit, which is a common and puzzling bench failure.

sections.heading: Series Resonance: When the Reactances Cancel
sections.body: Something remarkable happens to a series RLC circuit at the one frequency where the inductive and capacitive reactances are exactly equal in magnitude. Since they are opposite in sign, they cancel completely, the impedance collapses to the resistance alone, and the circuit behaves for that one frequency as if the inductor and capacitor were not there. Setting omega*L equal to 1/(omega*C) and solving gives the resonant angular frequency omega0 = 1/sqrt(L*C), or in hertz, f0 = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(L*C)). Notably the resistance does not appear: resonant frequency depends only on the inductance and capacitance. For the earlier example, L = 10 millihenries and C = 1 microfarad, the product L*C is 1e-8, its square root is 1e-4, and f0 = 1/(2*pi*1e-4), about 1592 hertz. At that frequency the impedance falls from the 108.6 ohms computed at 1 kilohertz to just the 50-ohm resistance, and the current rises from 92 milliamps to 200 milliamps, in phase with the source. A series resonant circuit is a frequency-selective short circuit. The dramatic part is what appears across the individual reactive components. At resonance the inductive reactance is 2*pi*1592*0.01, about 100 ohms. The 200-milliamp current through it produces 20 volts, and the same 20 volts appears across the capacitor with the opposite phase. The source is 10 volts. Twice the supply voltage stands across each reactive component, and they cancel exactly so Kirchhoff's law is satisfied. This voltage magnification factor is the quality factor, Q, and for a series circuit Q = omega0*L/R, equivalently (1/R)*sqrt(L/C). Here Q is 100/50, which is 2. With a higher Q the effect becomes spectacular and hazardous. Reduce the resistance to 1 ohm and Q becomes 100, so a 10-volt source produces a kilovolt across the capacitor. This is not a curiosity; it is the operating principle of the induction coil, of Tesla coils, and of the tuned input of a radio receiver, where a microvolt of antenna signal is magnified by a Q of a few hundred before amplification. It is also a genuine failure mode in power systems, where a resonance between line inductance and power-factor-correction capacitance, excited by a harmonic from a variable-speed drive, has destroyed capacitor banks. Q also determines selectivity. The bandwidth, defined between the two frequencies at which the current falls to 0.707 of its peak, is BW = f0/Q. A Q of 2 at 1592 hertz gives a 796-hertz bandwidth, which is very broad; a Q of 100 gives 15.9 hertz, sharp enough to separate adjacent broadcast stations. High Q means narrow, selective and strongly magnifying; low Q means broad, tolerant and gentle. Two design consequences follow directly. Because f0 depends on the product L*C but Q depends on the ratio of L to C, the same resonant frequency can be reached with many combinations, and the choice sets the impedance level and the achievable Q. A large inductor with a small capacitor gives a high-impedance, high-Q circuit; the reverse gives a low-impedance, heavily damped one. And because resistance alone sets Q while leaving f0 untouched, tuning and damping can be adjusted independently, which is exactly what makes the topology so tractable in design.

sections.heading: Parallel Resonance and the Tank Circuit
sections.body: Placing the inductor and capacitor in parallel rather than in series produces the mirror image: at resonance the impedance reaches a maximum rather than a minimum. The circuit is called a tank because energy sloshes back and forth between the magnetic field of the coil and the electric field of the capacitor, much as liquid oscillates in a vessel, with the external source needing to supply only the losses. The mechanism is best seen in admittances, which add for parallel elements. The capacitor's admittance is j*omega*C and the inductor's is 1/(j*omega*L), which is minus j/(omega*L). At the frequency where omega*C equals 1/(omega*L) they cancel, the total admittance of the reactive pair is zero, and the impedance is therefore infinite for an ideal lossless pair. The resonant frequency is the same expression as before, f0 = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(L*C)). Physically, large equal and opposite currents circulate around the loop between inductor and capacitor while almost no current is drawn from the source. In a series circuit Q magnifies voltage; in a parallel circuit Q magnifies current, and the circulating current is Q times the supply current. Real components have losses, overwhelmingly the winding resistance of the inductor, and this makes the peak impedance finite. The standard model places a small resistance r in series with L, and the resulting peak impedance, called the dynamic resistance, works out to approximately L/(C*r), which can also be written as Q*omega0*L or Q squared times r. For a 100-microhenry coil with 2 ohms of series resistance resonating with 250 picofarads at about 1 megahertz, the dynamic resistance is 100e-6 divided by (250e-12 times 2), which is 200 kilohms. A circuit built from a coil of 2 ohms presents 200 kilohms at one specific frequency and a few ohms everywhere else. That astonishing selectivity is why the parallel tank is the collector load in every traditional radio-frequency amplifier and the frequency-determining element in most oscillators. An important practical note is that a real inductor's Q is almost always the limiting factor. Capacitors of good dielectric routinely achieve Q values in the thousands, while a wound air-cored coil at a few megahertz might reach 200 and a small ferrite-cored one considerably less. Coil Q also varies strongly with frequency, rising initially and then falling as skin effect, proximity effect and core losses take over. When a resonant circuit underperforms, the inductor is the first suspect. Where very high Q is required, resonators of an entirely different physical kind are used instead: quartz crystals achieve Q values of 10,000 to over a million, which is why they, and not LC circuits, set the frequency of clocks and radio transmitters. A further practical consequence is that whatever the tank is connected to also loads it, so the loaded Q of a tank feeding a following stage is always lower than its unloaded Q, sometimes by a large factor.

sections.heading: Q, Bandwidth and Damping as One Idea
sections.body: The quality factor turns up in so many guises that it is worth assembling them into a single picture, because they are all the same number seen from different directions. Its most fundamental definition is energetic: Q equals 2*pi times the energy stored in the resonator divided by the energy dissipated per cycle. A resonator with Q of 100 loses about one sixty-third of its stored energy each cycle, since dividing by 2*pi turns the per-cycle fractional loss into 1/Q. This definition applies equally to an electrical tuned circuit, a pendulum, a tuning fork, a church bell, a quartz crystal and an optical cavity, and the numbers are instructive: a car suspension has a Q below 1 by design, a pendulum clock perhaps 10,000, a quartz watch crystal around 100,000, and the mirrors of a gravitational-wave detector far higher still. Its second face is the frequency-domain one: Q equals the resonant frequency divided by the half-power bandwidth, so a 10-megahertz circuit with Q of 50 has a 200-kilohertz bandwidth. Sharpness of tuning and lowness of loss are the same property. This is why a receiver cannot be made arbitrarily selective without consequence; narrowing the bandwidth to reject an adjacent station eventually starts to remove the sidebands carrying the wanted signal's information. Its third face is in the time domain. Struck with an impulse rather than driven with a sinusoid, a resonant circuit rings at approximately its resonant frequency with an amplitude decaying exponentially, and the number of cycles before the amplitude falls to about four per cent of its initial value is roughly Q. Control engineers prefer the reciprocal-like quantity called the damping ratio, zeta, related by zeta = 1/(2Q). A damping ratio below 1 gives an underdamped, ringing response; exactly 1 is critical damping, the fastest approach to the final value without overshoot; above 1 is overdamped and sluggish. A series RLC with R equal to twice the square root of L over C is critically damped, and this is precisely the calculation behind choosing a damping resistor to stop a relay driver or a probe compensation network from ringing. Seeing these as one idea pays off constantly. If a filter rings on a step input, its Q is too high, and the remedy is more loss. If an oscillator drifts or is noisy, its resonator Q is too low, and the remedy is a better resonator. If a tuned amplifier is too broad, adding a resistor deliberately across the tank will broaden it further in a controlled way, a technique called damping or loading, used routinely to flatten the response of intermediate-frequency stages at the cost of gain.

sections.heading: Real Components Are Not Ideal
sections.body: Every calculation above treats resistors, capacitors and inductors as pure. Real components are each a small network, and above a certain frequency the parasitic elements dominate the intended one. Ignoring this is the most common reason a design that simulates perfectly fails on the bench. A real capacitor has equivalent series resistance, arising from lead resistance, plate resistance and dielectric loss, and equivalent series inductance from its leads and internal geometry. The series inductance means every capacitor is itself a series resonant circuit with a self-resonant frequency, above which it behaves as an inductor. A through-hole 100-nanofarad ceramic capacitor with roughly 10 nanohenries of lead inductance self-resonates near 5 megahertz; a surface-mount version of the same value in an 0402 package, with perhaps 0.6 nanohenries, self-resonates above 20 megahertz. This is the real reason decoupling capacitors must be small packages placed close to the pin, and why several values in parallel are sometimes used, though that practice can create an anti-resonance between them that is worse than either alone. Electrolytic capacitors have comparatively enormous equivalent series resistance, often an ohm or more, which both limits their usefulness at frequency and causes them to heat internally under ripple current, the dominant failure mechanism in switching power supplies. A real inductor has winding resistance, which rises with frequency because of skin effect: alternating current crowds into a surface layer whose depth is about 66 micrometres in copper at 1 megahertz and 2.1 millimetres at 1 kilohertz, so above a few hundred kilohertz the interior of a thick wire carries almost nothing. It also has inter-winding capacitance, giving it too a self-resonant frequency above which it behaves as a capacitor, and if it has a magnetic core it has hysteresis and eddy-current losses that grow with frequency and flux and can drive the core into saturation, at which point the inductance collapses abruptly and non-linearly. Even a resistor is imperfect: wirewound types are frankly inductive, and any component's leads contribute roughly a nanohenry per millimetre. Beyond components, the circuit itself becomes a component. Once a conductor is a significant fraction of a wavelength, typically taken as more than about a twentieth, lumped analysis fails entirely and transmission-line theory with its characteristic impedance, reflections and standing waves must be used. A wavelength in free space is 300 metres at 1 megahertz but only 30 centimetres at 1 gigahertz, so a three-centimetre track is negligible in the first case and a significant transmission line in the second. Signals on a printed circuit board travel at roughly half to two-thirds the speed of light depending on the dielectric, which shortens the wavelength and brings the threshold closer than the free-space figure suggests. The practical discipline that follows is to know each component's self-resonant frequency and to stay well below it where the component is meant to behave as its nominal type. Manufacturers publish impedance-versus-frequency curves for exactly this purpose, and reading them is far more informative than reading the marked value. Much of what looks like mysterious high-frequency misbehaviour is simply a parasitic that was never on the schematic.

sections.heading: Measuring Impedance and Finding Resonance on the Bench
sections.body: Calculated values and real ones diverge, so measurement matters. The following procedure finds the actual resonant frequency and loaded Q of an LC circuit using ordinary equipment, and needs no specialist analyser. The principle is that a series resonant circuit's impedance dips to a minimum at resonance, so if it is fed through a known series resistor, the voltage across the resonant pair reaches a minimum, or across the resistor a maximum, at f0.
ingredients: A signal generator with a calibrated frequency readout, ideally sine output with adjustable amplitude; a cheap DDS module covering 1 hertz to a few megahertz is entirely adequate for audio and low radio-frequency work.
An oscilloscope, preferably dual channel so source and response can be compared directly, or an AC millivoltmeter if only magnitude is needed.
A known series resistor, typically 47 to 100 ohms, of 1 per cent tolerance, measured beforehand with a good ohmmeter.
The inductor and capacitor under test, plus a short length of wire and a solderless breadboard or, better at higher frequencies, a small piece of copper-clad board for a ground plane.
A frequency counter if the generator's own readout is not trustworthy; many inexpensive generators are several per cent out.
A x10 oscilloscope probe, which loads the circuit far less than a x1 probe.
steps: Measure the components individually first if you can, and note that a capacitor's marked value may be 20 per cent out and an inductor's more. Compute the expected resonant frequency from f0 = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(L*C)) so you know roughly where to look.

Wire the generator output through the known resistor into the series combination of L and C, with the far end returned to the generator ground. Keep the leads short, since stray inductance and capacitance shift the result.
Connect one oscilloscope channel across the generator output and the other across the resistor. The voltage across the resistor is proportional to the current through the circuit.

Set the generator to a modest amplitude, a volt or so peak-to-peak, and sweep slowly through the expected frequency, watching the resistor voltage. Adjust the generator amplitude as you go if its output is not flat with frequency, keeping the source constant.

Find the frequency of maximum resistor voltage. That is the true series resonant frequency f0. If it differs from the calculation by more than a few per cent, suspect the capacitor's tolerance or stray capacitance first.

Confirm resonance independently by checking phase: at f0 the current is exactly in phase with the source voltage, which on a dual-trace display means the two waveforms cross zero together, and on an X-Y display collapses the ellipse to a straight line.
Note the peak voltage, then find the two frequencies above and below at which it falls to 0.707 of that peak. Their difference is the bandwidth, and Q equals f0 divided by that bandwidth.

Remember that the measured Q is the loaded Q, degraded by your series resistor and by the probe. To estimate the component Q, repeat with a smaller series resistor and see how the figure changes; if it keeps rising, your measurement, not the circuit, is the limit.

sections.heading: Where the Method Breaks Down
sections.body: Phasor analysis is powerful precisely because it makes strong assumptions, and every one of those assumptions is a boundary beyond which the answers stop being trustworthy. Knowing where the boundaries lie is as important as knowing the technique. The first and most important assumption is linearity. Phasors require that doubling the input doubles the output and that superposition holds. Diodes, transistors driven beyond their small-signal range, saturating magnetic cores, and any component whose value changes with the applied voltage all violate this. Class II ceramic capacitors, the X5R and X7R dielectrics that dominate modern designs, can lose more than half their marked capacitance at their rated DC bias, which quietly shifts every corner and resonant frequency computed from the nameplate value. In a non-linear circuit, a sinusoidal input produces an output containing harmonics that were not present at the input, and the whole conceptual apparatus of a single-frequency impedance no longer applies. The usual remedy is to linearise about an operating point and analyse small signals, accepting that the result is valid only for small excursions. The second assumption is time-invariance. If component values change during the analysis, as in a switching converter where transistors reconfigure the topology tens of thousands of times a second, there is no single impedance to speak of. Such circuits are handled by averaging techniques or by simulation in the time domain. The third is the steady state. Phasors describe what happens after all transients have died away, which for a circuit of Q around 100 means many hundreds of cycles. They say nothing about switch-on surges, the inrush current of a transformer energised at the wrong point in the cycle, or the ringing that follows a step. Those require time-domain analysis, whether by differential equation, Laplace transform or simulation. The fourth is the single frequency. A distorted waveform must be decomposed into its Fourier components, each analysed separately at its own impedance, and the results recombined. This is not merely academic: harmonic currents from non-linear loads flow through impedances that rise with frequency, so the third and fifth harmonics of a 50-hertz supply can cause overheating in transformers and, in three-phase systems, dangerous currents in a neutral conductor sized on the assumption that the phases would cancel. Finally, a safety note that follows directly from resonance. Reactive voltage magnification is real, and a circuit fed from a modest supply can develop lethal or destructive voltages across an inductor or capacitor near resonance. Rate components for the voltage that will actually appear across them, not for the supply voltage, and treat any resonant circuit connected to the mains, whether deliberately or accidentally through power-factor capacitors, as capable of surprising you.

guides.title: Three-phase power systems
guides.summary: How three-phase electricity works: why three conductors carrying sine waves 120 degrees apart deliver smooth constant power, how wye and delta connections, transformers, motors and protection schemes are built on that idea, and how three-phase systems are measured, operated and diagnosed when they fail.

sections.heading: Why the World Runs on Three Phases
sections.body:
Almost every unit of electrical energy generated on Earth is produced, transmitted and consumed as three-phase alternating current. The lights in a house may be fed from a single pair of wires, but that pair is one leg tapped off a three-phase system that begins at the generator and runs unbroken through transmission towers, substations and street transformers. Understanding why the number is three, rather than one or two or six, explains most of what follows.

The problem three phases solve is that single-phase alternating power arrives in pulses. Voltage and current both swing sinusoidally through zero twice per cycle, so the instantaneous power delivered to a load also pulses, reaching zero a hundred or a hundred and twenty times a second and averaging only half its peak. A motor fed this way receives a torque that throbs at twice the supply frequency, which produces vibration, noise and mechanical fatigue, and a single-phase motor cannot start by itself at all without an auxiliary winding or capacitor to fake a second phase. A three-phase system, by contrast, delivers power that is mathematically constant in time when the load is balanced. The pulsations of the three phases interlock and cancel exactly, so a three-phase motor produces smooth torque and starts unaided.

The second advantage is economy of copper. To deliver a given amount of power at a given voltage and a given permissible power loss, three-phase transmission needs roughly seventy-five per cent of the conductor material a single-phase line would require, because the return currents of the three phases sum to zero and no dedicated return conductor is needed. Over a transmission corridor of hundreds of kilometres carrying gigawatts, that saving in aluminium, steel and tower strength is enormous. It was the decisive economic argument in the 1890s and it remains decisive today.

Three is the smallest number of phases that achieves both benefits. Two phases ninety degrees apart, a system genuinely built and briefly popular in the United States, produce a rotating field and can start a motor, but the instantaneous power still pulsates and the system needs four wires or three unequal ones. Six or twelve phases give marginal further smoothing at the cost of doubling or quadrupling the conductor count, which is why polyphase systems above three appear only inside specialised equipment such as large rectifiers, where twelve-pulse and twenty-four-pulse arrangements are created locally by transformer phase-shifting rather than transmitted across country.

The consequence is a global infrastructure of remarkable uniformity. Frequencies differ, at fifty hertz across most of the world and sixty hertz in the Americas and parts of Asia, and voltages differ, but the underlying architecture of three conductors carrying equal sinusoids displaced by one third of a cycle is essentially universal, and equipment designed against it interoperates across continents with only transformer and frequency adjustments.

sections.heading: Sinusoids, Phasors and the 120-Degree Displacement
sections.body:
A three-phase supply consists of three voltages of identical amplitude and frequency whose peaks are separated in time by one third of a cycle. If the phases are labelled A, B and C, and the peak line-to-neutral voltage is written as V with a subscript m, the three instantaneous voltages are V_m times the sine of the angle omega-t, V_m times the sine of omega-t minus 120 degrees, and V_m times the sine of omega-t minus 240 degrees. The angular frequency omega equals two pi times the supply frequency, so at fifty hertz one full cycle takes twenty milliseconds and the displacement between adjacent phases is 6.67 milliseconds. At sixty hertz the cycle is 16.67 milliseconds and the displacement 5.56 milliseconds.

The single most important algebraic fact about this arrangement is that the three voltages sum to zero at every instant. Adding sine of theta, sine of theta minus 120 and sine of theta minus 240 gives exactly zero for any theta, which can be checked by expanding each term or, more elegantly, by noticing that three unit vectors spaced evenly around a circle must sum to nothing because their arrangement has no preferred direction. This identity is why the neutral conductor of a balanced system carries no current, and it underlies almost every practical simplification in three-phase engineering.

Because handling three simultaneous sinusoids algebraically is tedious, engineers represent each as a phasor: a rotating vector whose length is the root-mean-square magnitude and whose angle is the phase displacement, with the rotation at supply frequency understood rather than drawn. In this representation a balanced three-phase set is simply three arrows of equal length at 0, minus 120 and minus 240 degrees, and the sum-to-zero identity becomes the visible fact that they close into an equilateral triangle. Adding two voltages becomes vector addition, and the phase shift introduced by an inductor or capacitor becomes a rotation.

The order in which the phases reach their peaks is called the phase sequence or phase rotation, and it matters enormously in practice. The sequence A-B-C, sometimes written as positive sequence, means B peaks after A and C after B. The reverse, A-C-B or negative sequence, is physically a mirror image, and connecting a motor to a supply of the wrong sequence makes it run backwards. Since a reversed pump, conveyor, saw or compressor can destroy equipment or injure people within seconds, phase sequence must be verified whenever a machine is connected or a supply is restored after work on the network. A phase rotation meter, a small instrument with three test leads and a rotating disc or an indicator lamp, does this in a few seconds and costs very little relative to the damage it prevents.

Root-mean-square values, not peaks, are used throughout power engineering because RMS is the value that produces the same heating in a resistor as an equivalent direct current. For a sinusoid, RMS equals the peak divided by the square root of two, about 0.707 times peak.

sections.heading: The Rotating Magnetic Field and the Birth of the System
sections.body:
The intellectual breakthrough that created three-phase power was the realisation that three coils arranged 120 degrees apart in space, fed by three currents 120 degrees apart in time, produce a magnetic field of constant magnitude that rotates smoothly around the machine. Nothing physically spins to make this field; it is a pattern that sweeps through the stationary iron as the currents rise and fall in sequence. Place a conductive rotor in that field and induced currents in it generate their own field, which the rotating field drags around. That is the induction motor, and it is arguably the most consequential electrical machine ever built.

Galileo Ferraris demonstrated a rotating field using two phases in Turin in 1885 and published in 1888, though he judged the arrangement to be of low efficiency and did not pursue commercial development. Nikola Tesla, working independently, filed the American patents in 1887 that were granted in 1888 and were bought by George Westinghouse, covering polyphase generation, transmission and motors. The specifically three-phase form, and the practical squirrel-cage rotor and star and delta connection arrangements that made it economic, were largely developed by Mikhail Dolivo-Dobrovolsky at AEG in Berlin between 1888 and 1891. He built the first three-phase induction motors, the first three-phase transformers and the first three-phase generators of usable size.

The decisive public demonstration came at the International Electrotechnical Exhibition in Frankfurt in 1891. A three-phase generator at a cement works in Lauffen am Neckar transmitted power 175 kilometres to Frankfurt at approximately 15,000 volts, driving a waterfall display and a thousand incandescent lamps. Measured efficiency exceeded seventy per cent, and later tests at higher voltage reached about seventy-five per cent. Nothing else available at the time could move power that far at that efficiency, and the demonstration settled the so-called war of the currents in favour of alternating current far more effectively than any argument.

The reason alternating current won is transformers. A transformer changes voltage with no moving parts and efficiencies above ninety-nine per cent in large units, but it works only on changing current. Transmission loss in a conductor is the current squared times the resistance, so raising voltage by a factor of ten to carry the same power reduces current by ten and loss by a hundred. Direct current at the time could not be transformed at all and so had to be generated near the load, limiting practical distribution radius to a couple of kilometres.

That historical logic remains the shape of the modern grid: generate at 11 to 25 kilovolts, step up immediately to 132, 275, 400 or 765 kilovolts for transmission, step down progressively through substations, and deliver at low voltage close to the customer. High-voltage direct current has since returned for very long links and undersea cables, using power electronics that did not exist in 1891, but it converts to and from three-phase alternating current at both ends.

sections.heading: Wye and Delta: The Two Ways to Connect Three Windings
sections.body:
Three windings, whether in a generator, a transformer or a load, can be joined together in exactly two topologies, and almost everything practical about a three-phase installation follows from which one is used where.

In the wye connection, also called the star connection and drawn with the letter Y or the Greek capital lambda, one end of each winding is joined to a common point called the star point or neutral, and the other end of each becomes a line terminal. The neutral may be brought out as a fourth conductor, earthed, or left floating. Because each winding sits between a line and the neutral, the voltage across it is the line-to-neutral voltage, and because each winding is in series with its own line conductor, the current through it is the full line current.

In the delta connection, drawn as a triangle and written with the Greek capital delta, the three windings are joined end to end in a closed loop, and the three junctions become the line terminals. There is no neutral point at all. Each winding now sits directly between two lines, so it sees the full line-to-line voltage, but the line current arriving at a corner splits between two windings, so each winding carries less than the line current.

The choice has real engineering consequences. Wye gives access to two voltages from one system, which is why low-voltage distribution is almost universally wye: a 400 volt three-phase supply in Europe provides 230 volts between any line and neutral for lighting and sockets, and the 208 volt system in North America provides 120 volts the same way. Wye also provides a neutral point that can be earthed, which fixes the potential of the whole system relative to ground, limits the voltage stress on insulation, and gives earth-fault current a defined return path so that protective devices operate.

Delta has no neutral and therefore cannot supply line-to-neutral loads, but it has a compensating virtue: it provides a closed circulating path for third-harmonic and zero-sequence currents, which keeps those currents inside the delta rather than letting them distort the supply or flow into the earth. Delta windings are also mechanically robust in a fault, and a delta-connected bank can continue to operate at fifty-seven point seven per cent of rated capacity with one winding removed, an arrangement called open delta or V connection that is genuinely used for emergency continuity.

In practice most equipment uses both. A distribution transformer is typically delta on the high-voltage side and wye with an earthed neutral on the low-voltage side, giving harmonic containment upstream and a usable neutral downstream. A three-phase motor is often wound so it can be connected either way, allowing the star-delta starting method that reduces inrush current during acceleration.

sections.heading: The Square Root of Three and How to Use It
sections.body:
The number 1.732, the square root of three, appears in every three-phase calculation, and it is worth understanding where it comes from rather than memorising it as a magic constant.

Consider a wye-connected source with 230 volts between each line and the neutral. The voltage between two lines is not 460 volts, because the two phase voltages are not opposed; they are 120 degrees apart. Subtracting one phasor from another that is 120 degrees away produces a resultant whose length is 2 times 230 times the cosine of 30 degrees, and since the cosine of 30 degrees is 0.866, the result is 230 times 1.732, or 398 volts, which is why the European low-voltage standard is quoted as 400 over 230 volts. The same geometry gives 208 over 120 volts in North America, 480 over 277 volts for American commercial buildings, and 690 over 400 volts for large industrial drives.

The rules that follow are compact. In a wye connection, line voltage equals the square root of three times phase voltage, while line current equals phase current. In a delta connection, line voltage equals phase voltage, while line current equals the square root of three times phase current. In both cases total three-phase apparent power is the square root of three times line voltage times line current, and real power is that quantity multiplied by the power factor, the cosine of the angle between voltage and current in each phase.

A worked example fixes the ideas. A three-phase motor is rated 30 kilowatts at 400 volts with a power factor of 0.86 and an efficiency of 0.92. The electrical input power is 30 divided by 0.92, which is 32.6 kilowatts. Line current is input power divided by the product of the square root of three, line voltage and power factor: 32,600 divided by 1.732 times 400 times 0.86, which is 32,600 divided by 596, giving 54.7 amperes. That single calculation determines the cable size, the fuse or breaker rating and the contactor selection, and getting it wrong is the most common error in small installation work.

Two useful shortcuts follow. At 400 volts, a three-phase load draws approximately 1.7 amperes per kilowatt at unity power factor, so a rough current estimate is kilowatts times 1.7 divided by power factor. At 208 volts the figure is about 2.8 amperes per kilowatt, and at 480 volts about 1.2. Second, the same load connected in delta draws three times the current and three times the power of the identical load connected in wye on the same supply, because each winding sees the square root of three times the voltage and current scales with voltage in a linear load. This three-to-one ratio is precisely the basis of star-delta motor starting, where the machine is accelerated in wye at one third of the delta inrush current and then switched over once it approaches speed.

sections.heading: Power, Power Factor and Why Instantaneous Power Is Constant
sections.body:
In any alternating-current circuit three different quantities are all loosely called power, and confusing them is the source of endless practical trouble. Real power, measured in watts or kilowatts, is the rate at which energy is actually converted into work, heat or light, and it is what a meter bills. Reactive power, measured in volt-amperes reactive, is energy that sloshes back and forth between the supply and the magnetic or electric fields of inductors and capacitors, doing no net work but occupying conductor capacity. Apparent power, in volt-amperes, is simply the product of voltage and current and represents the burden the load actually imposes on cables, transformers and switchgear. The three are related by a right triangle: apparent power squared equals real power squared plus reactive power squared. Power factor is real divided by apparent, equal to the cosine of the phase angle in a purely sinusoidal circuit.

The distinctive feature of a balanced three-phase system is that its total instantaneous power does not vary with time. Instantaneous power in one phase is the product of its instantaneous voltage and current, which for sinusoids expands into a constant term plus a term oscillating at twice supply frequency. When the three phases are summed, the constant terms add to three times the per-phase average, while the three double-frequency terms are themselves 120 degrees apart in the doubled angle and therefore sum to exactly zero. The result is a steady flow of power with no ripple at all, which is why three-phase machinery runs so much more smoothly than single-phase.

This constancy is genuinely conditional. It holds only when the three phases are balanced in magnitude and displacement and the waveform is sinusoidal. Unbalance or harmonic distortion reintroduces pulsating terms, producing torque ripple in motors, vibration and additional heating.

Poor power factor is expensive even though reactive power does no work, because the current that carries it heats every conductor it passes through. A factory drawing 500 kilowatts at a power factor of 0.70 pulls 714 kilovolt-amperes and therefore 1,030 amperes at 400 volts. Correcting the power factor to 0.95 reduces apparent power to 526 kilovolt-amperes and current to 760 amperes, a twenty-six per cent reduction that cuts cable losses by nearly half, since losses go as current squared. Most industrial tariffs therefore penalise low power factor directly.

Correction is normally achieved with capacitor banks connected in delta across the supply, sized in kilovolt-amperes reactive, and switched in stages by a controller that monitors the instantaneous power factor. Care is needed: capacitors and the supply inductance form a resonant circuit, and if that resonance lands near a harmonic frequency present in the plant, currents can be amplified severely. Detuning reactors in series with the capacitors shift the resonance away from harmful frequencies and are standard practice wherever variable-speed drives are installed.

sections.heading: Generators: How Three-Phase Electricity Is Made
sections.body:
Nearly all bulk electrical energy comes from synchronous alternators, machines whose output frequency is rigidly tied to their shaft speed. The stationary outer part, the stator, carries three sets of windings physically distributed around the bore and displaced by 120 electrical degrees. The rotating inner part, the rotor, carries an electromagnet energised with direct current through slip rings or, in modern machines, through a brushless exciter mounted on the same shaft. As the rotor turns, its magnetic field sweeps past each stator winding in turn and induces in it a sinusoidal voltage, the three windings producing the three phases automatically by virtue of their spacing.

Frequency is set by speed and pole count according to a simple relation: frequency in hertz equals the shaft speed in revolutions per minute times the number of pole pairs, divided by sixty. A two-pole machine, one pole pair, must therefore turn at 3,000 revolutions per minute for fifty hertz or 3,600 for sixty hertz, which is why steam and gas turbine sets run at those speeds. Hydroelectric turbines run far slower, often 100 to 500 revolutions per minute, and compensate with many poles: a 60 rpm hydro generator on a fifty hertz system needs fifty pole pairs, giving it the characteristic large-diameter, short-axial-length shape.

Voltage is controlled by the rotor excitation current, which is adjusted by an automatic voltage regulator. Increasing excitation raises the generated voltage and, when the machine is connected to a stiff grid whose voltage it cannot move, instead causes it to export reactive power. Real power output is controlled entirely separately, by the mechanical torque the turbine applies to the shaft, mediated by a governor that responds to system frequency. This clean separation, real power by throttle and reactive power by excitation, is the basis of grid control.

Connecting a generator to a live system, called synchronising, requires four conditions to be met simultaneously: identical frequency, identical voltage magnitude, identical phase sequence and near-zero phase angle difference at the moment the breaker closes. Getting this wrong is spectacular and destructive. Closing 180 degrees out of phase applies twice rated voltage across the machine and can produce a torque transient that shears the coupling or bends the shaft. Synchroscopes, check-synchronising relays and automatic synchronisers exist precisely to prevent this, and the modern standard practice is to close only when the slip is small, the angle within about ten degrees, and the voltage difference under a few per cent.

Once connected, generators on a grid are locked together electrically. If one tries to speed up, its rotor angle advances, it exports more power, and the resulting retarding torque pulls it back. This self-regulating synchronising torque is what allows thousands of machines across a continent to run in lockstep, and its progressive loss under severe disturbance is what produces the cascading instability seen in major blackouts.

sections.heading: Three-Phase Transformers and Vector Groups
sections.body:
A three-phase transformer can be built either as three separate single-phase units connected together, common in the very largest transmission ratings where a spare single unit is cheaper than a spare three-phase one, or as a single core with three limbs sharing a common magnetic circuit, which is lighter, cheaper and standard for everything up to several hundred megavolt-amperes. In the three-limb design the fluxes of the three phases sum to zero in the yokes exactly as the currents do, so no separate return path for flux is needed, and the saving in iron is substantial.

Primary and secondary can each be wye or delta independently, giving four basic combinations, and the choice profoundly affects behaviour. Delta-wye, written Dy, is the workhorse of distribution: the delta primary traps triplen harmonic currents and blocks zero-sequence current from passing upstream, while the wye secondary supplies a neutral for single-phase loads. Wye-delta, Yd, is used for stepping down at the transmission end. Delta-delta, Dd, provides no neutral either side but tolerates open-delta operation. Wye-wye, Yy, is the least common in isolation because without a delta somewhere the magnetising current cannot flow properly and the neutral point can shift badly under unbalanced load; when it is used, a third winding in delta, called a tertiary or stabilising winding, is normally added.

Every wye-delta or delta-wye connection introduces a phase displacement between primary and secondary of thirty degrees or an odd multiple of it. This is captured in the vector group notation, a code such as Dyn11, in which the capital letter is the high-voltage winding configuration, the lower-case letter the low-voltage one, the letter n indicates that the low-voltage neutral is brought out, and the number is the phase displacement expressed in clock-face hours, each hour equalling thirty degrees. Dyn11 therefore means delta high-voltage, wye low-voltage with neutral available, and the low-voltage vector lagging or leading by thirty degrees as though at eleven o'clock.

The practical importance is absolute: transformers cannot be paralleled unless their vector groups are compatible. Connecting a Dyn11 in parallel with a Dyn1 puts sixty degrees of phase difference across the connection and drives a circulating current limited only by the impedance of the two transformers, which is to say an effective short circuit. Paralleling also requires matched voltage ratios, and percentage impedances within a few per cent of each other so that load shares in proportion to rating rather than dumping onto whichever unit has the lower impedance.

Two further connections deserve mention. The zigzag or interconnected-star winding splits each phase between two limbs to create an artificial neutral with low zero-sequence impedance, used for earthing otherwise unearthed systems. The Scott-T connection uses two specially tapped transformers to convert three-phase into two-phase, historically for two-phase legacy loads and still used for balanced single-phase supply to electric railways.

sections.heading: The Induction Motor: The System's Reason for Existing
sections.body:
The three-phase induction motor consumes something close to half of all electricity generated worldwide, and its extraordinary simplicity explains why. The stator carries three windings that create the rotating field. The rotor, in the overwhelmingly common squirrel-cage form, is nothing but a stack of laminated steel discs with conducting bars of aluminium or copper cast into slots near its surface and short-circuited by end rings. There are no brushes, no commutator, no slip rings and no electrical connection to the rotor whatsoever. The only wearing parts are two bearings.

The physics is elegant. The stator field rotates at synchronous speed, given by 120 times the supply frequency divided by the number of poles, so a four-pole machine on fifty hertz has a synchronous speed of 1,500 revolutions per minute and on sixty hertz 1,800. If the rotor were turning at exactly that speed it would see no relative motion, no changing flux, no induced current and therefore no torque. So it cannot; it must lag. The fractional difference is called slip, and at full load it is typically two to five per cent, giving a four-pole fifty hertz motor a real running speed around 1,440 revolutions per minute. The relative motion induces currents in the rotor bars, those currents interact with the stator field, and the resulting force drags the rotor along.

Torque rises with slip up to a maximum called breakdown or pull-out torque, typically two to three times rated torque, and then falls again. If the mechanical load exceeds breakdown torque, the motor stalls, slip goes to one hundred per cent, and current rises to the locked-rotor value of five to eight times rated. That current will destroy the windings within tens of seconds, which is why thermal overload protection is mandatory rather than optional.

Starting current is the machine's principal nuisance. Direct-on-line starting draws six to eight times full-load current for the second or two of acceleration, which on a large motor can dip the supply voltage enough to dim lights across a site or drop out contactors. Mitigations in ascending order of cost and sophistication are star-delta starting, which reduces starting current to a third but also torque to a third and imposes a transient at changeover; autotransformer starting; soft starters using thyristors to ramp the applied voltage; and variable-frequency drives, which rectify the incoming three-phase to direct current and re-synthesise a three-phase output of adjustable frequency and voltage.

The variable-frequency drive has become the default for anything larger than a few kilowatts, because it starts the motor at essentially rated current, allows speed control, and on centrifugal pumps and fans delivers dramatic energy savings, since flow varies with speed but power varies with roughly the cube of speed. Reducing a fan to eighty per cent speed cuts its power to about half. Against that, drives generate harmonics and high-frequency switching stress on winding insulation and bearings, which is why inverter-duty motors and shaft grounding rings exist.

sections.heading: Distribution Architecture, Neutrals and Earthing
sections.body:
Between the generator and the socket, three-phase power passes through a hierarchy of voltages, each chosen to trade conductor cost against insulation and clearance cost. Generation is typically at 11 to 25 kilovolts, limited by what can be insulated inside a rotating machine. Immediately adjacent step-up transformers raise this to transmission levels of 132, 220, 275, 400 or in some countries 765 kilovolts. Subtransmission runs at 33 to 132 kilovolts, primary distribution at 11 to 33 kilovolts, and final distribution transformers deliver low voltage at 400 over 230 volts, 208 over 120 volts or 480 over 277 volts depending on the country and the application.

The neutral conductor exists to carry the imbalance current from single-phase loads. In a perfectly balanced four-wire system it carries nothing, but real buildings never balance perfectly, and the neutral must be sized for the worst realistic case. Historic practice of running a reduced-size neutral is now discouraged, and in circuits feeding substantial non-linear load the neutral may need to be larger than the phase conductors for reasons discussed in the context of harmonics.

How the system is connected to earth is one of the most consequential design decisions in an installation, and several distinct philosophies coexist. A solidly earthed system bonds the transformer star point directly to earth, so an earth fault produces a large current that operates protection quickly and definitively; this is standard for low-voltage distribution. A resistance-earthed system inserts a resistor sized to limit earth fault current to perhaps 5 to 400 amperes, enough to be detected reliably but small enough to avoid arc damage and to allow a controlled shutdown, common in industrial medium-voltage plants. An unearthed or high-impedance system, called IT in the international classification, has no deliberate earth connection at all, so a single earth fault causes almost no current and the plant keeps running while an insulation monitoring device raises an alarm; this is used in hospital operating theatres, mines and shipboard systems where an unplanned trip is more dangerous than a fault.

The letter codes TN-S, TN-C-S and TT describe how the earth reference reaches the consumer. In TN-S the neutral and protective earth are separate all the way from the transformer. In TN-C-S, widely used in Britain as protective multiple earthing, they share one combined conductor in the supply cable and separate at the intake. In TT the consumer provides an independent earth electrode and relies on residual current devices for protection, because the earth loop impedance is too high for a fuse to clear a fault reliably.

The distinction matters at the point of use. A broken combined neutral-earth conductor in a TN-C-S supply can put the full phase voltage onto the earthed metalwork of an installation, which is the specific reason that connecting electric vehicle chargers and outbuildings under that arrangement requires dedicated open-conductor detection or a separate earth rod.

sections.heading: Unbalance and the Method of Symmetrical Components
sections.body:
Real systems are never perfectly balanced. Single-phase loads are unevenly distributed, cable impedances differ slightly, and faults are frequently asymmetric, affecting one or two phases rather than all three. Analysing such systems directly is awkward, because the elegant simplifications of balanced operation all evaporate.

The tool that rescues the situation was published by Charles Fortescue in 1918 and is called the method of symmetrical components. Its central claim is that any set of three unbalanced phasors can be decomposed uniquely into the sum of three balanced sets: a positive-sequence set of three equal phasors in normal A-B-C rotation, a negative-sequence set of three equal phasors in reversed A-C-B rotation, and a zero-sequence set of three equal phasors all in phase with each other. Add the three sets back together phase by phase and the original unbalanced quantities reappear exactly.

The power of this decomposition is that each sequence network can be analysed separately, using ordinary balanced-circuit techniques, and the results superposed. Machines and lines have different impedances to each sequence, and those differences are physically meaningful. Positive-sequence current produces the normal forward-rotating field. Negative-sequence current produces a field rotating backwards at synchronous speed, which in a motor or generator rotor appears at twice supply frequency and induces large eddy currents that heat the rotor severely; this is why generators have strict negative-sequence withstand limits and why even modest voltage unbalance is damaging. Zero-sequence current is identical in all three phases, so it cannot flow at all unless a return path exists through a neutral or earth, which is precisely why a delta winding blocks it and why zero-sequence measurement is the basis of earth-fault detection.

The practical consequences are direct and quantitative. Voltage unbalance, defined as the maximum deviation from the average line voltage divided by that average and expressed as a percentage, is generally limited to two per cent for distribution systems and one per cent at motor terminals. The effect on motors is disproportionate: a rough engineering rule is that percentage current unbalance is six to ten times percentage voltage unbalance, and a two per cent voltage unbalance can raise winding temperature by around twenty-five per cent, roughly halving insulation life because insulation ageing follows an approximately exponential relation in which every ten degrees Celsius of additional temperature halves life. Standards accordingly require motors to be derated when unbalance exceeds one per cent and prohibit operation above five per cent.

Diagnosing unbalance means measuring all three line currents and all three line voltages, not one of each. A single clamp meter reading tells nothing about balance. Where unbalance is found, the usual causes are unevenly distributed single-phase loads, a high-resistance connection in one phase, a failing transformer tap, an open delta bank, or an incipient winding fault, and they are distinguished by whether the unbalance follows the load or stays with the phase.

sections.heading: Harmonics and the Triplen Neutral Problem
sections.body:
Everything described so far assumes pure sinusoids. Modern electrical loads mostly do not draw sinusoidal current. Switch-mode power supplies in computers, LED drivers, electronic ballasts, uninterruptible power supplies and the front-end rectifiers of variable-speed drives all draw current in short high peaks near the voltage crest, charging a capacitor and then drawing nothing until the next peak. Fourier analysis expresses such a distorted waveform as a fundamental at supply frequency plus a series of harmonics at integer multiples.

Harmonics are classified by their sequence, and the pattern is regular. The fifth, eleventh and seventeenth harmonics form negative-sequence sets and produce backwards-rotating fields that create braking torque and rotor heating in motors. The seventh, thirteenth and nineteenth are positive sequence. The third, ninth, fifteenth and twenty-first, collectively called the triplen harmonics, are zero sequence, meaning they are in phase in all three conductors.

This last fact produces a genuinely counterintuitive and dangerous consequence. Fundamental currents in a balanced four-wire system cancel in the neutral. Triplen currents do not cancel; they add arithmetically. Three phases each carrying the same third-harmonic current send three times that current down the shared neutral. In an office building or data centre densely populated with single-phase electronic loads, neutral current can therefore exceed phase current, sometimes reaching 1.5 to 1.7 times it. A neutral sized on the historic assumption that it need only handle imbalance will then overheat, and because the neutral is not usually protected by an overcurrent device the overheating is undetected until insulation fails. Standards now require the neutral in such circuits to be full-sized or oversized, and specify derating factors for cables carrying significant triplen content.

Distortion is quantified by total harmonic distortion, the root-sum-square of all harmonic components expressed as a percentage of the fundamental. Voltage distortion above five per cent at the point of common coupling is generally considered the limit for public supplies, with individual harmonics limited to three per cent. Current distortion limits depend on the ratio between short-circuit capacity and load current, on the principle that a stiff supply can absorb more distortion without the voltage waveform suffering.

Mitigation exists at several levels. Delta transformer windings trap triplen currents in the delta and prevent them from propagating upstream, which is the single most effective structural measure. Line reactors or direct-current link chokes ahead of a drive raise its source impedance and cut its current distortion from perhaps eighty per cent down to thirty-five. Passive tuned filters, capacitors in series with reactors resonant at a chosen harmonic, sink specific frequencies. Active harmonic filters measure the distorted current and inject its inverse in real time, handling multiple harmonics and changing loads but at substantially greater cost. Twelve-pulse and eighteen-pulse rectifier arrangements use phase-shifting transformers to cancel the lowest harmonics inherently, and are common at large drive ratings.

sections.heading: Measuring Three-Phase Power in Practice
sections.body:
Metering a three-phase supply is less obvious than metering a single-phase one, and the governing principle is Blondel's theorem, stated by André Blondel in 1893: to measure power in a system of n conductors, n minus 1 wattmeters are sufficient, provided the common reference point for the voltage coils is placed on the omitted conductor. A four-wire wye system with a neutral therefore needs three wattmeters, referenced to the neutral. A three-wire system, whether delta or an unearthed wye, needs only two, and this two-wattmeter method works regardless of balance or waveform, which surprises people the first time they meet it.

In the two-wattmeter arrangement the current coils go in two of the three lines, and both voltage coils reference the third. The algebraic sum of the two readings is the total three-phase real power, and one of the readings will go negative when the power factor falls below 0.5, which is a legitimate result rather than an instrument fault. The ratio of the two readings also encodes power factor, so the method yields it without separate measurement.

Modern practice mostly bypasses all this with a three-phase power quality analyser, which samples all voltages and currents thousands of times per cycle and computes real, reactive and apparent power, power factor, unbalance and harmonic spectra directly. Current is measured with clamp-on current transformers for steady loads or Rogowski coils, flexible air-cored loops that impose no saturation limit, for high currents and transient work.
steps: Establish that the system is safe to work on and that you are competent and authorised. Wear appropriate arc-rated clothing and use a meter with the correct category rating for the voltage and available fault energy at that point.

Identify the system type before touching anything: count the conductors, find the neutral if one exists, and confirm whether the supply is wye or delta. Measure line-to-line and line-to-neutral voltages to confirm; on a 400 volt wye you expect roughly 400 between lines and 230 to neutral.
Verify phase rotation with a rotation meter before connecting any rotating machine, and label the phases physically so the result is not lost.
Measure all three line-to-line voltages and calculate unbalance as the largest deviation from the average divided by the average. Anything above two per cent needs investigation before proceeding.

Clamp each of the three line conductors in turn and record the currents, then, if a neutral exists, clamp that too. Neutral current above about one third of the phase current on a linear installation points to unbalance; neutral current approaching or exceeding phase current points to triplen harmonics.
Record power factor and total harmonic distortion for both voltage and current, and note the load condition at which the readings were taken, since all of these vary with load.

Compare measured full-load current against the nameplate value calculated as power divided by root three times voltage times power factor times efficiency, and investigate any discrepancy greater than about ten per cent.

sections.heading: Faults, Fault Levels and Protection
sections.body:
A short circuit on a three-phase system releases energy at a rate limited only by the impedance between the fault and the generators feeding it. The prospective short-circuit current at a point, often called the fault level and quoted either in kiloamperes or in megavolt-amperes, is the single most important number for selecting switchgear, because a breaker asked to interrupt more current than it is rated for will fail, sometimes explosively.

Fault levels are calculated by reducing the network to an equivalent impedance seen from the fault point. A useful approximation for a low-voltage installation is that fault current at the transformer secondary terminals equals the transformer's rated current divided by its percentage impedance expressed as a fraction. A 1,000 kilovolt-ampere transformer at 400 volts has a rated current of about 1,443 amperes; with a typical impedance of five per cent, the fault level at its terminals is roughly 29 kiloamperes. Cable impedance downstream reduces this quickly, which is why fault levels fall as one moves away from the source.

Faults come in several types with markedly different currents. Three-phase symmetrical faults are the rarest but usually the most severe and are the design case for switchgear rating. Single-line-to-earth faults are by far the most common, accounting for roughly seventy to eighty per cent of all faults on overhead systems, and their magnitude depends heavily on the earthing arrangement. Line-to-line and double-line-to-earth faults fall in between. Sequence-component analysis handles all of them systematically, which is the practical reason the technique is taught.

Protection is arranged in graded layers so that the device nearest the fault operates first and the minimum amount of the system is disconnected, a principle called discrimination or selectivity. Fuses and inverse-time overcurrent relays achieve this by time grading, with upstream devices set slower. Differential protection compares current entering and leaving a zone such as a transformer or busbar and trips on any difference, giving instantaneous and absolutely selective operation within its zone. Distance protection measures the apparent impedance seen from a line end and trips if it falls inside a set reach, which is standard on transmission circuits. Earth-fault protection detects zero-sequence current, either by summing the three phase currents in a core-balance transformer or by measuring residual current.

Arc flash deserves separate emphasis because it kills people who were never in contact with a live conductor. An arcing fault in a switchboard converts electrical energy into a plasma at temperatures around 19,000 degrees Celsius, with a pressure wave and molten metal spray. Incident energy is calculated in calories per square centimetre, with 1.2 calories being the threshold for a second-degree burn on bare skin. Protective clothing is specified against that calculated value, and the most effective mitigation is reducing clearing time, since incident energy scales roughly linearly with arc duration.

sections.heading: Characteristic Failure Modes and How They Present
sections.body:
Three-phase systems fail in a small number of recognisable ways, and learning to read the symptoms saves both equipment and diagnostic time.

Single-phasing is the loss of one phase while the other two remain energised, caused by a blown fuse, a failed contactor pole, a broken conductor or a loose terminal. A running three-phase motor does not stop when this happens; it continues to turn on the remaining two phases, producing reduced torque while drawing roughly 1.7 to 2 times its rated current in those phases. Winding temperature rises rapidly and the machine burns out in minutes if unprotected, and the failure is characteristically confined to particular coil groups, which is how a rewind shop identifies the cause afterwards. A motor that has not yet started when a phase is lost will not start at all; it will sit humming and drawing locked-rotor current. Simple thermal overloads may or may not catch this in time, which is why dedicated phase-failure and phase-unbalance relays are standard on motors of any consequence.

Phase reversal occurs after any work that disturbs the supply connections, and its effect is immediate: pumps run backwards and deliver nothing while cavitating, compressors run backwards and destroy themselves, conveyors and lifts move the wrong way, and machine tools can injure operators. The defence is procedural rather than technical, namely to verify rotation with a meter after every intervention rather than trusting the wire colours, which are frequently wrong in older installations.

A lost or high-resistance neutral in a four-wire wye system is the most destructive common fault in low-voltage distribution. With the neutral intact, each single-phase load sits at a fixed line-to-neutral voltage. With the neutral broken, the loads on the three phases become a series network across the line voltages, and the star point of the load floats to wherever the impedances dictate. Lightly loaded phases rise toward line voltage, in a 400 volt system meaning appliances designed for 230 volts see 300, 350 or more, while heavily loaded phases sag. The typical presentation is lights burning unnaturally bright in one part of a building and dim in another, followed by a wave of simultaneous equipment failures. Any report of that pattern should be treated as urgent.

Ferroresonance is a rarer but genuinely confusing failure in which the non-linear magnetising inductance of a transformer resonates with cable or grading capacitance, usually after single-pole switching or a blown fuse on a lightly loaded transformer. It produces sustained overvoltages of two to three times nominal, loud irregular humming from the core, chaotic waveforms that sometimes audibly beat, and surge arrester failure. It does not decay on its own, because the supply itself sustains the resonance, and the remedy is to break the circuit and re-energise all three poles together.

sections.heading: Working Safely and Systematic Troubleshooting
sections.body:
Three-phase equipment kills through three distinct mechanisms, and each demands its own precaution. Electrocution requires only a few tens of milliamperes through the chest, and 230 volts is entirely sufficient. Arc flash burns and its associated blast injure people standing near a fault without any contact. Stored energy in capacitors, in the direct-current link of a variable-speed drive, and in the excitation circuits of large machines remains lethal after the supply is removed, which is why drive manuals specify a wait of five to fifteen minutes before opening the enclosure.

Safe isolation is a defined sequence, not an attitude. Identify the correct circuit and confirm it by tracing rather than by label. Isolate with a device capable of breaking load. Secure the isolation with a personal lock and tag so nobody else can restore supply. Prove your voltage tester on a known live source or a proving unit. Test between every pair of conductors and from every conductor to earth, not just across the pair you expect to matter. Prove the tester again afterwards, because a tester that failed during the test would have shown dead throughout. Only then apply earths where the system or procedure requires them.

Fault diagnosis rewards a structured approach. Begin by establishing what the system is doing rather than what it should do, and by measuring all three phases of both voltage and current rather than sampling one. Compare the pattern against the recognised failure modes: symptoms that follow a particular phase when the load is moved indicate a supply-side problem, while symptoms that follow the load indicate an equipment problem. Thermal imaging finds loose or corroded connections quickly and safely, since a joint carrying normal current with elevated resistance runs measurably hot, and a rise of ten to twenty degrees Celsius above its neighbours is a clear indication. Insulation resistance testing at 500 or 1,000 volts direct current, with the result corrected to a standard temperature, tracks winding and cable degradation over time, and a trend downward matters far more than any single absolute value.

Certain failures should never be reset without investigation. A tripped breaker on a circuit that has run reliably has told you something. Repeated resetting into a fault is a recognised cause of arc flash injury, because each attempt re-establishes the fault current with the operator standing at the panel.

Finally, three-phase work is legally regulated nearly everywhere. Beyond the smallest domestic tasks it requires demonstrated competence, and connection to the public network is restricted to authorised persons.
